title: What Is Functional Language?
brief: Define functional language as the fixed and semi-fixed expressions people use to perform social actions with words — requesting, apologizing, inviting, agreeing, greeting, and so on. Draw on the Dialogs source, which describes its 30 dialogs as focusing on 'a wide variety of communicative and natural encounters in English,' to illustrate that language does things in real situations. Explain the distinction between a grammatical structure and a communicative function: the same function (e.g., making a suggestion) can be expressed through several different forms, as seen in the Dialogs source where 'Why don't we practice those dialogs together?' serves as a suggestion rather than a genuine question. Introduce the idea that fixed expressions like 'Good idea' or 'Guess what!' carry meaning that cannot be derived from their individual words alone.

title: Functions in Action: A Tour of the Dialogs
brief: Walk through a selection of the 30 situational dialogs from the Dialogs source to show the range of functions covered: formal and informal greetings and farewells (Dialogs 1 and 2), formal and informal introductions (Dialogs 3 and 4), expressing effort and encouragement (Dialog 30), and sharing news (the dialog containing 'Guess what!'). For each example, identify the communicative function being performed and highlight the specific fixed or semi-fixed expression that carries it — for instance, 'I give up' for abandoning effort, 'Really?' as an animated rejoinder, and 'Just think…' to signal reflection. Show how a single dialog can contain multiple functions layered together, preparing teachers to notice this complexity in authentic exchanges.

title: Language Notes as a Teaching Tool
brief: Explain how the Language Notes that accompany each dialog in the Dialogs source model the kind of metalinguistic awareness teachers need when presenting functional language. Use specific examples from the source: the note that 'Really?' does not question truthfulness but expresses animated interest; that 'They'd like' is 'a little softer, a little less positive, than they want'; and that 'Simply' means 'absolutely, completely, clearly.' Show teachers how these notes reveal the pragmatic and connotative layers of fixed expressions — layers that grammar rules alone cannot capture — and discuss how teachers can adapt this annotation approach when preparing their own functional-language materials for class.

title: An Introduction to Idiom
brief: Introduce idiom as a category of fixed expression whose meaning is not predictable from its component words, using examples drawn directly from the Dialogs source Language Notes: 'Give up' is glossed as 'stop trying; abandon effort,' and 'Set a date' means 'decided on a day when it will take place.' Distinguish idioms from other fixed expressions by showing that their meaning is opaque without contextual explanation, whereas a phrase like 'Good idea' is transparent. Use the Dialogs source note on verb repetition ('I try and try') to illustrate a related semi-fixed pattern that intensifies meaning through repetition rather than through idiomatic opacity. Emphasize that idioms, like other functional expressions, are best learned in the situations where they naturally occur.

title: Why Functions Matter Alongside Grammar
brief: Argue that grammar knowledge alone does not equip learners to participate in real communicative encounters, drawing on the Dialogs source description of dialogs that focus on 'communicative and natural encounters in English' and are accompanied by notes on 'grammar and intonation patterns.' Use the contrast between grammatical correctness and communicative appropriateness: a learner may form a grammatically perfect sentence yet choose the wrong level of formality, as illustrated by the Dialogs source distinction between formal and informal greetings (Dialogs 1 and 2) and between formal and informal introductions (Dialogs 3 and 4). Connect this to the Shaping source's point that a student-centered classroom for speaking involves students understanding 'why they are doing particular activities' and 'what they will be gaining or learning from them,' reinforcing that functional purpose should be transparent to learners.

title: Teaching Functional Language from Situations
brief: Present a situation-first approach to teaching functional language, grounded in the Dialogs source model of short situational dialogs that embed expressions in a clear social context before any analysis takes place. Describe a teaching sequence: present the situation and dialog, have learners identify what social action is being performed, then draw attention to the specific expressions used, using Language Notes-style commentary to unpack meaning and register. Reference the Dialogs source note that the book allows for 'self-directed study programs' via audio, and connect this to the Shaping source's mention of students practicing dialogs and listening to tapes while filling in blanks, as one classroom technique. Close by advising teachers to build a bank of short situational dialogs organized by function — greetings, suggestions, encouragement, sharing news — so that learners encounter functional expressions repeatedly across varied contexts.
